patch.value: The dependency token budget is enforced against a different representation than the one emitted, so a command that reports staying inside 16k tokens delivers about 45k

pm deps enforces a 16,000-token budget, reports that it stopped because it hit that budget, and then emits output that is roughly 2.8 times the budget it just enforced. Measured on three separate hub items on 2026-07-26: pm-96h7 emits 177,608 bytes against estimated_tokens 16,011; pm-doxj emits 181,745 against 16,015; pm-mpbb emits 179,441 against 15,991. Every one of them reports truncation with reasons max_depth and token_budget, so the ceiling is being applied — it is simply applied to something other than what is printed. Applying the estimator's own heuristic to the bytes it actually emitted gives 44,402, 45,436 and 44,860 tokens respectively, so the disagreement is internal and needs no external tokenizer to demonstrate. The ratio is stable at 11.1 to 11.4 emitted bytes per budgeted token where the estimator assumes 4, which points at a systematic accounting error rather than a per-item outlier. The mechanism is visible in the estimator itself: estimateTokens in src/sdk/relationship-context.ts:175 measures JSON.stringify of an individual node or edge object, while the rendered tree carries the full item payload for every retained node. The budget is therefore computed over a different representation than the one delivered to the caller. The consequence is that the entire budget contract is unfalsifiable as specified: a corpus gate that asserts commands against their declared budgets, which is the enforcement mechanism pm-5t33or plans, would pass on all three of these calls while the caller pays nearly three times the declared ceiling.

The enforced estimate is computed over the representation that is actually emitted, per output format, rather than over an intermediate node or edge object; A test asserts that emitted output size and the reported estimate agree within a declared tolerance for every budgeted command and every format; Where an exact tokenizer is impractical, the declared tolerance is stated in the contract so callers know the error bound instead of assuming none; Truncation disclosure reports the real retained cost, so a caller reading the envelope can size a follow-up request correctly; The fix covers tree, graph and context formats, since each renders a different amount per retained node; Existing default budgets are re-derived after the accounting is corrected, so correcting the measurement does not silently shrink every answer
Make a declared output budget mean the size of what the caller actually receives
Token budgets become enforceable rather than decorative, which is the precondition for every downstream budget gate
Removes a roughly threefold silent overspend on the most graph-heavy read surface and repairs the premise of the budget contract
Budget accounting measures the rendered payload, disclosed truncation reflects real cost, and a regression test pins the estimate against the emitted bytes
The terminal graph backfill has substantially increased edge density, so every under-counted traversal now costs more than when the estimator was written
